Title: The Untouchables: Why Corporate Criminals Never Go to Prison

Summary: 
The article exposes a systemic pattern in which corporate executives avoid criminal punishment while ordinary offenders receive harsh sentences. It cites the 2008 Lehman Brothers collapse, where $10 trillion of wealth was destroyed and 8 million jobs lost, and notes that the bank hid $50 billion in toxic assets through the ‘Repo 105’ scheme with the help of lawyers at Linklaters. Despite this, no Lehman executive has been imprisoned. The piece highlights a ‘revolving door’ in which 67 % of senior DOJ prosecutors who leave government between 2016 and 2023 join defense firms that represent the same corporations they once investigated, often after declining to prosecute major cases citing ‘insufficient evidence’. The article names Mary Jo White, who pioneered deferred prosecution agreements (DPAs) as U.S. Attorney and later defended the same banks at Debevoise & Plimpton. It explains that since 2000 the DOJ has signed over 500 DPAs while prosecuting fewer than 100 executives, allowing companies to pay fines and avoid criminal convictions. Specific examples include HSBC’s 2012 DPA for laundering $881 million, which cost the bank $1.9 billion, and Boeing’s 2021 DPA for the 737 MAX crashes that killed 346 people, costing $2.5 billion with no executive charges. The article argues that corporate lawyers use complexity to defeat prosecution, citing the 2008 financial crisis instruments and a federal judge’s remark that ‘Corporate crime has become so sophisticated that our legal system can’t process it. By the time prosecutors understand the scheme, statutes of limitations have expired.’ In contrast, the article notes that in 2023 400 000 Americans were incarcerated for drug offenses, many for amounts under $100, while Purdue Pharma executives extracted $11 billion and received probation. It concludes that the two‑tier justice system erodes public trust, quoting Senator Elizabeth Warren: ‘When criminals in corporate suites walk free while those on street corners go to prison, people lose faith in justice.’ The piece calls for structural reform to break the prosecution‑to‑defense pipeline.

Title: Be prepared for the new corporate liability rules

Summary: 
The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 introduces a new failure‑to‑prevent fraud offence for larger organisations and reforms the corporate liability rule, known as the attribution principle, making all companies—including SMEs—strictly liable for economic crimes committed by senior managers. The rule covers money laundering, VAT and customs duty evasion, bribery and sanctions breaches, and applies regardless of whether the offence benefits the company. Under the new law, a company can be prosecuted on a strict‑liability basis if a senior manager commits an offence, and the usual failure‑to‑prevent bribery defence is no longer available. Senior managers are defined broadly, including anyone in the direct chain of management or in strategic or compliance roles, irrespective of title, remuneration, qualifications or employment status; the article notes, 'It is not limited to those who perform an executive function or serve as board members.' Companies can avoid prosecution by confessing early and paying a civil penalty, but otherwise face potential dismissal, fines, imprisonment and director disqualification. The article urges directors to adopt proactive compliance training and to make senior managers aware of the new legal reality, recommending the UK Government’s failure‑to‑prevent guidance as a starting point for SMEs.

Published date: September 30 2025, 09:10

Source: The Scotsman

Title: Dos años de prisión para seis exdirectivos de la ACA por usar información reservada

Summary: 
The Barcelona High Court has rejected the cassation appeals against a 2022 ruling that sentenced six former executives of the Catalan Water Agency (ACA) to two years in prison each. Four were convicted of disclosing confidential information, and two were convicted of using such information to influence public procurement decisions. The misconduct involved the awarding of a consultancy contract titled 'Works for the Preparation of the Measures Program and the Management Plan of the Catalan River Basin District.' The court ruled the procurement process was 'irregular' and fraudulent, as it violated principles of publicity and free competition required by public contracting regulations. The court found that the defendants, despite being aware of their duty of confidentiality as public officials, coordinated to share privileged information about the upcoming tender, which benefited a consortium (UTE) that included a company linked to one of the accused. The decision confirms that the contract was improperly awarded through the misuse of confidential data.

Citation key: [9]
Title: Affaire de corruption IMETAL : 25 cadres devant le juge dans un scandale à plusieurs milliards

Summary: 
The trial for the major corruption scandal involving the Algerian public industrial group Imetal, specializing in metal and steel industries, is set to begin on November 24, 2025, before the economic and financial criminal court in Algiers. The date was confirmed by the court president after a defense-requested postponement to appoint new lawyers, marking the final delay before the trial's opening. The case involves 25 individuals, including former Imetal and Sider El Hadjar executives, public and private officials, and other high-level figures, charged with serious offenses. According to the investigation dossier, the scandal emerged from a detailed report submitted to the prosecutor revealing massive management irregularities. The report accuses senior officials of manipulating tenders, signing illegal contracts, and favoring certain companies at the expense of public interest. The allegations center on two key subsidiaries: the Sider El Hadjar steel complex in Annaba and the National Recovery Company (ENR). Investigators allege an organized system of fund diversion, distorted competition, and undue financial benefits, leading to significant production declines and repeated plant failures. These practices reportedly caused substantial financial harm to the state-owned enterprise and the national treasury. On March 12, 2023, the investigating judge ordered provisional detention for Imetal’s CEO, T.B., who died in prison on July 4, 2023, along with four other senior executives, including the CEO of Sider. Seventeen others—managers, intermediaries, and businessmen—were also charged. The investigation uncovered a network of internal and external corruption involving pressure and blackmail to secure public contracts in Algeria and abroad. The highly anticipated trial aims to expose the mechanisms of embezzlement and favoritism that weakened one of Algeria’s key industrial assets. Observers view the Imetal affair as emblematic of opaque governance and the severe economic consequences of systemic corruption in the public sector.

Published date: November 03 2025, 20:05
